title: Alkynes
note: Terminal alkynes (pKa about 25) are deprotonated by NaNH₂, and the acetylide ion alkylates methyl and primary halides by SN2, building longer chains. Hydration gives an enol that tautomerizes to a ketone (HgSO₄, Markovnikov) or to an aldehyde (hydroboration). Reduction stops at a cis alkene with Lindlar's catalyst and a trans alkene with Na in NH₃.

read.title: Building chains from acetylene
text: An alkyne has two π bonds, so it undergoes many of the same additions as an alkene, often twice. One equivalent of HBr gives a vinyl bromide; a second equivalent adds to the same carbon and gives a geminal dibromide. Water adds in the presence of acid and a mercury(II) catalyst. The first product is an enol, with OH on a doubly bonded carbon, but the enol quickly tautomerizes to the more stable ketone. A terminal alkyne gives a methyl ketone by this route, while hydroboration with a bulky borane gives an aldehyde instead.

Reduction can be controlled. Hydrogen with an ordinary palladium catalyst goes all the way to the alkane. Lindlar's poisoned catalyst stops at the alkene and adds both hydrogens from one face, giving a cis alkene. Sodium in liquid ammonia adds electrons one at a time and produces the trans alkene.

The C–H of a terminal alkyne is unusually acidic for a hydrocarbon. Sodium amide removes it to give an acetylide anion, a strong nucleophile. With methyl or primary alkyl halides it forms a new C–C bond by SN2, which makes alkynes useful starting points for synthesis. Secondary and tertiary halides fail, because the strongly basic acetylide causes E2 elimination instead.
